title: Firefighters 'shook up' after planned burn destroys fire tanker
text:
An investigation has been launched into a hazard reduction burn in Sydney's south-west that caused the destruction of a fire truck and the hospitalisation of a smoke-affected firefighter.

Conducted by the New South Wales Rural Fire Service, the planned burn at Wedderburn started at 10am Saturday after two successful test fires.

The fire intensified at about 4pm following a sudden change in wind conditions, with the blaze destroying one fire tanker and damaging two others.

The fire intensified after conditions changed, causing minor property damage. (ABC News)

An RFS volunteer firefighter suffered smoke inhalation and chest pain during the incident and was taken to hospital as a precaution. He has since been released.

Seventeen other volunteer firefighters were assessed and cleared by paramedics.

Additional resources, including two helicopters, were sent to regain control of the fire.

Crews returned to the site on Sunday to continue with damage assessments, with minor damage reported at two properties.

Crews shaken

RFS Commissioner Trent Curtin said the crews activated emergency spray systems on the tankers after becoming overrun by fire.

"Our firefighters are well-trained and they activated their training and their fire protection systems to look after themselves at the time," Commissioner Curtin said on Sunday.

"I understand that some of our crews were away from their tanker at the time that the fire came through, they retreated to a property nearby and admirably undertook firefighting operations immediately after retreating from that area."

Commissioner Trent Curtin says crews activated emergency spray systems on the tankers. (ABC News)

Commissioner Curtin said affected volunteers continued to receive support, including from chaplains and critical incident personnel.

"You can imagine that they are shook up and our crews are concerned about the incident that occurred," he said.

"But what happens is very, very quickly those crews wrap around themselves, they wrap around each other and we provide additional support."

Authorities won't say whether the incident could have been prevented. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Commissioner Curtin said it was too early to say if the incident could have been prevented, with investigations into the circumstances of the fire ongoing.

"I launched an investigation that will look into all of the factors of this hazard reduction burn to make sure that we can learn everything about what happened yesterday, and that we take action to make that these conditions don't happen again," he said.

"There is some risk in undertaking hazard reduction burning, there is risk in firefighting and we'll look into all the elements of that as part of the investigation."

'Heightened fire risk'

Commissioner Curtin said fire authorities continued to prepare for "what might be a heightened fire risk this bushfire season".

"We've had the driest winter on record, we've got strong El Niño conditions confirmed," he said.

Commissioner Curtin says conditions have been drier than average. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

"We know that we're going to see high temperatures and dry conditions through the spring period and that may lead into the summer period.

"Everybody should have a bushfire survival plan, and download the Hazards Near Me app to make sure that they're notified when a fire does occur in their area."

The safety regulator has been notified of the Wedderburn incident.

title: Brisbane's Story Bridge to close over new year for maintenance
text:
Brisbane's iconic Story Bridge is set to close for three weeks over the new year for maintenance.

The repairs include resurfacing the southern approach and parts of the northern approach, as well as structural deck maintenance and waterproofing.

The bridge, which carried up to 100,000 vehicles a day, according to Brisbane City Council, is scheduled to close from Sunday, December 27, 2026, to Monday, January 18, 2027.

Brisbane City Council's Ryan Murphy said the repairs were part of $110 million in funding under the Operation Smooth program.

"Big part of that is the road surface, Brisbane residents who have driven over the approaches from the northern and southern side of the story bridge recently would have noticed it's getting a little bit bumpy," Cr Murphy said.

"We will be going in over the summer to resurface.

"It will be a hot, sweaty and arduous job, but it's necessary in order to preserve this asset."

Ryan Murphy says the repairs will be hot and sweaty. (ABC News: Emma Johnson)

Council hoped the closure would coincide with a time when Brisbane residents were away for the summer holidays.

Alternative routes included the Captain Cook Bridge, the Go Between Bridge, the Clem7, the Gateway Bridge and the William Jolly Bridge.

The maintenance comes amid discussions about whether the Story Bridge could return to being a toll bridge if a funding deal to restore it could not be reached, according to Brisbane City Council.

An independent committee found the 85-year-old bridge would be unable to carry traffic within 20 years without a full restoration, at a cost it said would be "beyond council".

The committee suggested several ways to fund the restoration, including a toll similar to the one on the Sydney Harbour Bridge, contributions from council and state and federal governments, an annual rates levy or corporate sponsorship.

Previously, Brisbane City Council said in a statement that a toll or levy would only be considered as a "last resort".

title: Retiree travelling 18,000km around Australia on electric motorcycle
text:
There is no petrol tank, no spare battery and in some parts of Australia, barely a town in sight.

Retired electrical engineer Ed Darmanin, from Sydney, has spent the past three months riding an electric motorcycle around some of the country's most remote roads, carefully calculating every kilometre between charging points.

As the 67-year-old rides from Frankston to Lakes Entrance through Gippsland this week, he is nearing the end of an 18,000-kilometre journey.

He is understood to be the first person to ride around mainland Australia on an electric motorcycle.

Ed Darmanin's trip around Australia started and ends in Sydney. (Supplied)

Mr Darmanin spent five years embarking on electric motorcycle journeys that had never been done before, including becoming the first to cross Australia by electric motorcycle and later riding from Sydney to Darwin via Birdsville.

He said completing an Australian first was part of the motivation behind his latest adventure.

"To be first was something I've wanted to do for years," Mr Darmanin said.

"I really wanted an adventure, a challenging adventure.

"And being a retired electrical engineer and understanding EV technology, because I've been driving EV cars since 2015, I know how it all works, and it takes a lot of planning to do this."

His latest journey began in Sydney on June 24, travelling anti-clockwise around the country on his Energica Experia and visiting every mainland state and territory.

Ed Darmanin is doing some sections of the 18,000km journey with his wife and son. (Supplied)

He has ridden parts of the journey with his wife Sally and son Evan, while completing the remaining parts solo.

Mr Darmanin said the biggest challenge was ensuring the motorcycle had enough energy to cover each leg.

"You can't carry a spare battery; that's just built into the bike. It's sort of like carrying a spare engine on a normal motorcycle, you just can't do it," he said.

"So it's all about planning; the planning includes just looking at where the available DC fast chargers are, which are the same fast chargers that the EV cars use, and my bike can use those as well."

Carefully crafted charging plans

The motorcycle's range is affected by speed, with Mr Darmanin sometimes having to slow down to make it between charging points.

"The battery in the bike is probably only around one-quarter of the size or one-third of the size of most electric vehicles," he said.

"And if you sat on 100km/h on a straight, flat road like in the outback, you'd probably only get about 160km with all the luggage and everything on the bike.

"But the distances were up to 260km. In fact, there were a couple that were 300."

Ed Darmanin is visiting every state and territory on mainland Australia. (Supplied)

Mr Darmanin said travelling at a slower speed could make a significant difference to how much energy the bike used.

"If I sat on 110km/h compared to 75km/h, at 110 you use double the energy or double the fuel," he said.

That careful planning has been particularly important in remote parts of the country, where there can be hundreds of kilometres between services.

"When you leave that town, it's 260km until you get to the first roadhouse, and there is absolutely nothing between those two spots," Mr Darmanin said.

Strong headwinds across the Nullarbor Plain forced Mr Darmanin to postpone crossing by two days, while his previous journey to Darwin included a 390km stretch of mostly unsealed road through remote country.

Ed Darminan started the journey in June. (Supplied)

After thousands of kilometres, Mr Darmanin said he was beginning to appreciate how significant the journey had become.

"I'm starting to realise it's quite an achievement, and I like to share the story for that reason," he said.

"It's complementary to the fact that I've ticked off a major bucket-list item."

With the final stretch through south-eastern Victoria's Gippsland region before the ride back to Sydney, the finish line is finally in sight.

Mr Darmanin has shared his journey on his website, highlighting his stops and reflecting on the experience.

title: How the Lions claimed their moments to overcome a dominant Freo
text:
The footy season is a marathon, not a sprint.

Each game goes for about three hours, a long amount of time in our increasingly attention starved society. Multiply that by the 218 games over several months and the time starts to add up.

Especially if you are in one of the highest profile jobs in footy.

"The level of intensity that's required to be a senior coach, because it is a lifestyle, it never leaves you alone," premiership winning coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final.

In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

"It's 365 days a year, seven days a week. It's just always in your head. You're always thinking about the club and what's next."

In the era of short form video and instant takes, being involved in football nearly forces you to do the opposite.

You don't scroll through football games, you absorb them.

But football games, especially important ones, aren't one continuous event. They are made up of a series of moments and contests that separate the winner from the loser.

The bigger the stakes, the more important those discrete moments are. It's also something that newly minted three-time premiership coach Fagan has previously attested to.

"Finals come down to moments," Fagan told afl.com.au in 2020.

It was a theme he has repeatedly come back to, year after year. Win enough of those moments at the right time and you might just win the premiership. It's a formula that the Lions have ridden to their spot as maybe the most successful side of the modern era.

The importance of moments is something that wasn't lost on his opposite number coming into the finals.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained earlier in September.

Those moments also turned the 2026 grand final into one of the greatest in recent history. It was in those moments that the two-time champion Lions became three-time champions.

By winning enough moments at the right time Brisbane was able to overcome the biggest lead in time-on in a final since at least 2001.

Much of the 2026 grand final played out the way that the 2026 season had progressed, with Fremantle in control. On paper, Fremantle not just dominated proceedings but played in a way that took away Brisbane's strengths.

"Fremantle deserved to win that game today. They were better," Fagan said.

"They were better than us for longer periods. They were killing us at clearance and contested possession, particularly in that third quarter and we couldn't get any territory. They had a lot of inside 50s. They had more shots."

On paper, Fremantle should have won the game and done so comfortably.

But Brisbane won the moments that mattered.

"It's a little bit like this group has become this team that seems to need to get themselves into a dire situation before they can actually produce their best," Fagan said.

This is how Brisbane won the 2026 grand final.

A tight first half

It wasn't just a late swing that made the game a classic. This year's grand final had twists and turns almost from the first bounce. The first half saw nine lead changes through the first two stanzas, with the two sides often trading goals.

Despite this, more things were breaking Fremantle's way than Brisbane's early.

In the first half Fremantle was able to control the game in ways that Brisbane usually thrive. The Dockers were able to effectively neutralise the Lions' usually strong clearance game through the first half, both gaining position and hitting the scoreboard.

While the Lions broke even at around the ground stoppages, the Dockers were able to dominate centre clearances and piled on three goals from the middle.

The Dockers were also able to effectively outmanoeuvre the Lions in the air. The Lions have traditionally had the best mark differential of any team, with Fremantle one of the few to seriously challenge them.

However Fremantle dominated the marking battle, with their tall timber taking the upper hand. Fremantle also seemed to find a way to isolate Brisbane's shaky defence, with Patrick Voss seemingly finding a weak spot in their defensive set up.

Even when the Lions were able to dominate field position — such as the ten minute or so burst in the middle of the second quarter — they were unable to pile on the points.

The only thing keeping the Lions in the game was their maniacal forward half pressure. The Lions managed nine first half tackles inside their own 50 to just two from the Dockers. Brisbane was also able to translate this into a four goal edge in front half intercept scoring in the half.

At the end of the first half, the margin was the same before a ball was kicked in anger. Instead of four quarters to decide the premier, there would be just two.

The back end

For much of the third quarter it looked like the control Fremantle were able to exert on the game was starting to pay off on the scoreboard. While the game still stayed within a couple of goals, Brisbane didn't look out of it.

That was until Fremantle piled on 14 points in around five minutes, seemingly creating enough of a barrier to preserve the Flagmantle dream.

Some things slowly started to turn Brisbane's way despite the Dockers looking like they were gaining an unassailable lead. The Lions were slowly able to gain ascendancy in the air, managing 15 marks on the lead in the second half to nil.

They were also slowly able to quell Caleb Serong's gigantic influence on the game, particularly at stoppage. After collecting 12 clearances in the first three quarters Serong managed just one in the final period.

Most importantly the Lions started to work out how to pierce the league's best defence absent its most important piece — captain Alex Pearce.

"We had to play a bit smaller and we missed his leadership across the back end of the game and clearly missed his leadership late. He gives us so much in that aspect of the game," Longmuir said after the game about Pearce's game-ending Achilles injury.

Before the injury Brisbane managed just one goal from set shots, with three coming after the injury. The Lions struggled to move the ball effectively up ground before his injury, but found the paths to goal over time. It's also easy to imagine how Pearce would have settled the ship once it started going down fast in the end.

Of course, those last four minutes are the things dreams — and nightmares — are made of. Will Ashcroft winning three straight centre clearances from the same spot, with every Lion rising around the young star.

The moments and the missed missed opportunities

In the end it's the moments that will resonate the longest after this magical grand final. We will remember how Ashcroft won the ball in the middle late, and how LOgan Morris kicked straight. We will remember Josh Dunkley's defensive prowess and Ryan Lester's last ditch effort to save a goal.

Brisbane didn't have any passengers, nor did Fremantle. That's what made the Norm Smith Medal so hard to choose this year, and so controversial.

Unfortunately the memories for Fremantle will be more bitter than sweet. If they had to map out what the perfect game would look like for them — scoring aside — it would have looked something like what played out in the end.

"Obviously for you know four quarters we played "Fremantle football" and it's the last two minutes we didn't take our moments," Norm Smith medallist Shai Bolton said after the game.

For now, it's Brisbane's day to celebrate yet again. Especially those four minutes and 18 seconds in the last quarter where Brisbane overcame Fremantle, a seventeen point deficit and, yes, Wharfie Time to cement their place as one of the greatest teams in football history.

title: Brisbane Festival 2026: Our favourite shows
text:
Brisbane Festival has wrapped up for another year, with the month of September bringing an incredible range of events to the river city.

There's been something for everybody, from world-slaying nostalgia acts to out-of-the-box theatrical creations, and everything in between.

All part of Brisbane's ambitious push to become a true world city ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, the festival has centred the creative verve of Queensland and beyond on the shores of the Brisbane River.

More than 1.7 million people attended ticketed and free events produced by almost 2,000 artists over the course of the festival, including 535,000 people who visited the festival village at South Bank.

Artistic director Ebony Bott said her first year at the helm had seen the festival's box office haul jump 46 per cent from 2025.

"There has been a generosity and an openness in the way Brisbane has responded that has been incredibly moving to witness," Ms Bott said.

"I'm immensely proud of what we've made, but more than anything, I'm leaving these weeks with an even greater sense of what is possible here."

Here are seven shows we caught at Brisbane Festival in 2026.

title: Thousands rally against Spain's housing crisis after 87yo's eviction
text:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets in Madrid to protest against Spain's housing crisis and ask for protective measures for tenants, anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.

The protest on Saturday came in reaction to the dramatic eviction on Wednesday of an 87-year-old woman from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for decades.

"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse.

"And we can't keep maintaining this.

" Housing is a right and we don't have it. "

Taken out of her home on a stretcher in the upscale Retiro neighborhood, María del Carmen Abascal was greeted by protesters and supporters as she was loaded into an ambulance.

Some demonstrators held up their house keys as they protested for more housing rights. (Reuters: Alejandro Martinez Velez)

Spanish media reported that Ms Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a rent cap.

The building changed ownership in 2018, and Ms Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants' Union, which organised Saturday's protest.

Incomes have not kept pace with rising costs in Spain, leaving many out of the housing market. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($810) to 2,650 euros ($4290).

It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros ($2670), which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.

Courts blocked three previous attempts to evict her.

Extensive media coverage turned Ms Abascal into a symbol of Spain's housing crisis.

Demonstrators hold a banner reading "Not one Maricarmen more" in support of the evicted pensioner. (Reuters: Alejandro Martinez Velez)

"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.

"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted."

At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza with apparent plans to stay put.

Loading...

Some even pitched tents to stay at least the night or until police forcibly removed them.

Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market, despite strong economic growth in Europe's fourth-largest economy.

Incomes have not kept pace. Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply.

At the end of the march, some demonstrators set up a camp at the Puerta del Sol square. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share.

Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for public rental housing, which represents less than 2 per cent of its available supply.

The European Union average is 8 per cent.

Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownership, removing them from the public housing stock.

"I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," Ms Abascal said on Friday.

She spoke from her hospital bed after the eviction in a video shared by the tenants' union.

title: Cyclist 'died eight times' before getting a new heart
text:
Wollongong cyclist Cameron Butcher likes to say he has nine lives.

After he had a pacemaker installed in his early 20s, he recorded the eight times it saved his life.

The first came at just age 22 when the device shocked his heart back into rhythm as he lay unconscious on the grass after picking up a frisbee.

Things became even more serious when he experienced four shocks in the space of 10 minutes.

Cameron in hospital after receiving his new heart. (Supplied)

"The heart kind of just gave out and I was put on the transplant list," Mr Butcher said.

" A week later I got the call to go in and get a new heart. "

Nearly two years on from his heart transplant, the 26-year-old elite cyclist is the fittest he's ever been and is competing in the Australian Transplant Games which kicked off in Launceston on Saturday.

The long road to a diagnosis

As a 20-year-old, Mr Butcher was mountain biking and road racing around Australia until he was struck down by severe fatigue.

He was initially misdiagnosed with poor liver function, but over time his symptoms continued to worsen.

"They found I was having three seconds between heartbeats and my left ventricle, which is the one that sends blood out to the rest of the body, had become really inflamed and enlarged and wasn't doing its job," he said.

Cameron Butcher got back on the bike just five weeks after his heart transplant. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Tests revealed Mr Butcher's heart was working at about a third of normal capacity.

A pacemaker was implanted but his heart began to fail.

Confronting his mortality at 24 was something he never expected.

"Getting that diagnosis of heart failure was probably the best thing that happened to me because for two and a half years I was trying to work out what was wrong," Mr Butcher said.

"I died eight times, so I always tell people I have nine lives."

Remarkable recovery

Less than five weeks after his transplant, Mr Butcher was back on the bike.

Cameron trains on Mount Keira in the Illawarra. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

"The first week [after the transplant] wasn't too pleasant," he said.

"But by the second week I was up [walking] and about doing 15 laps of the ward per day.

" I'm now the fittest I've ever been. "

Within six months, he won the mixed relay section of the 2025 Peoplecare Triathlon in Wollongong.

He also placed second at the 2025 Road Nationals in the transplant category, and won his age group in the 60-kilometre Willo Mountain Bike Race in March.

Celebration of life

The biennial transplant games is an Olympic-style sporting event for those who have undergone a transplant.

They were first organised by British transplant surgeon Dr Maurice Slapak in 1978 after he became inspired by a kidney recipient he ran with.

Chris Thomas, the CEO of Transplant Australia. (ABC Sport: Chris Taylor)

Chief executive of Transplant Australia Chris Thomas described the event as a celebration of life.

"Every participant owes their life to someone else," he said.

"They're people who were really once at death's door contemplating their future and then miraculously, someone has given them an organ to enable them to live.

"It's a really good opportunity to bring our community together to learn from one another."

Cameron Butcher with his mum post-heart transplant. (Supplied)

Mr Butcher will be competing in cycling, tennis, swimming and six-a-side soccer.

"I'm really competitive about the cycling stuff, but the other stuff's just a bit of fun and never been to Tassie before," he said.

The games will run until October 3.

title: Small businesses under pressure as Canberrans weigh up cost of living
text:
The CEO of the Canberra Business Chamber is confident when he says business sentiment in the territory is currently "as bad as it's ever been".

The Reserve Bank is expected to raise interest rates a fourth time this year to manage inflation, in part from high fuel prices spurred on by the war in the Middle East, along with Australia's tight jobs market. At the moment, Canberrans are copping the highest fuel prices of all Australian capital cities.

Canberra Business Chamber CEO Greg Harford said businesses felt pressure was mounting when simultaneously, consumers were not spending as much.

"The cost of running a business is up, just as the cost of running a household is up," Mr Harford said.

Canberra is currently the most expensive capital city in the country for both petrol and diesel. (ABC News: Tahlia Roy)

"You've got interest rates, the cost of petrol, all of that's really biting consumers' disposable income," he said.

"So there's less money coming in the door for many businesses, and that obviously puts real pressure on profitability in some of those areas."

Retail, hospitality, services hardest hit

Mr Harford said the coming expansion of portable long service leave to the hospitality and retail sector, while benefiting employees, was an example of rising costs which could ultimately be passed onto consumers.

Canberra's peak body for businesses fears the retail and hospitality sectors are the most vulnerable to increasing costs. (ABC News: Elise Pianegonda)

Under the portable long service scheme, casual workers have access to long service entitlements, even if they switch employers. Employers register and pay a set levy on the gross ordinary wages of eligible employees.

Mr Harford also said Canberra's commercial property rates had gone up about 8 per cent this year.

Greg Harford says business sentiment is the worst he has seen. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"My real worry is for those small businesses that are heavily leveraged, they've got very small margins, they're very reliant on customers coming through the door and spending, and those are the ones that are most at risk in the current situation," he said.

Pet surrenders continue

Animal shelters around the country have been under strain as Australians weigh up living expenses with the cost of companion animals.

The RSPCA says it is common for people to give up their pets to manage daily living costs. (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

In the ACT since 2022, the cost of living has been one of the main reasons Canberrans were handing in their companion animals, according to the RSPCA.

"'Unable to afford care' was the seventh most common surrender reason in FY22, but it has consistently ranked among the highest reasons in more recent years, including being the second most common reason for the past two years," Canberra's local RSPCA said.

title: What is Wharfie Time and how did it backfire for heartbroken Dockers?
text:
As the bells tolled around the MCG on Saturday, Fremantle fans screamed in exhilaration.

This was finally their moment in the premiership sun after 31 long years of waiting.

Wharfie Time had arrived, and with four minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, there was surely no way that the Dockers could bottle this one — particularly with their viral celebration in full swing.

And then it all fell apart.

What is Wharfie Time?

You will no doubt have heard about it by now.

Before this year the phrase "Wharfie Time" would likely never have passed your ears, and now it's all the AFL world can talk about.

Wharfie Time is a viral celebration the Dockers have been using sparingly in close games at Perth Stadium during the 2026 season.

It's only ever used after a Fremantle goal, it's only ever used once in a game, and it's designed to get the crowd up and about to inspire the Fremantle players to see the game out as strongly as possible.

The lights in the stadium dim, leaving only an eerie glow of purple, as the bells from ACDC's song Hells Bells toll through the stadium and the words "Wharfie Time" appear on the big screen.

The Dockers have recently gone all-in on embracing ACDC, with former lead singer Bon Scott buried in the area due to his family emigrating there when he was young.

A guitarist at the top of the stadium starts every game playing Hells Bells, with the whole show being Fremantle's answer to the after goal songs that the Brisbane Lions do, or Port Adelaide fans singing INXS's Never Tear Us Apart before a game.

But what does the phrase 'Wharfie Time' even mean?

Great question.

It all goes back to former Dockers skipper and now Sydney Swans boss Matthew Pavlich using the phrase in a pre-match rev up in 2009.

Pavlich was mic'd up before the match and was caught telling his teammates "put on your Superman capes boys, it's Wharfie Time", as can be seen at the 39 second mark of the video below.

When it happened nobody really knew what the hell he was talking about. The "Wharfie" part was in reference to the dock workers and the club's mascot being the Dockers, but mixing it with Superman capes reference was a little … odd.

It went down in viral footy moments folklore, on par with Brett Kirk's infamous "Thanks Basil" speech.

The Dockers went on to embrace the quirkiness of it all and started the Wharfie Time celebration this year.

How did it backfire in the grand final?

In the lead-up to the match there had been a heap of talk around whether the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time at the MCG.

The Lions and the Cats had been allowed to use their goal celebrations in the 2025 grand final, with Charlie Cameron's Take Me Home, Country Roads celebration a particular fan favourite, often appearing to lift the Lions when they needed it most.

On the morning of the grand final, it was finally properly confirmed — the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time in the 2026 decider.

Just after confirmation, Brisbane football manager Danny Daly confirmed to ABC Sport's Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron that coach Chris Fagan had played the tolling bells to his Lions players in their Friday afternoon meeting. He didn't elaborate further.

We then witnessed one of the great grand finals in the history of the game.

After an incredible to-and-fro throughout, with 4 minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, Fremantle's Patrick Voss kicked a goal to put the Dockers up by 17 points.

The bells started to toll. Dockers fans went wild. It felt as if the end was nigh.

And the Lions came back from the dead.

Legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews has always said that he thinks the absolute limit of how many goals a team can kick in a particular amount of time is one goal per minute left.

Four minutes left. Four goals for the Lions. Heartbreak for the Dockers.

Several Lions players would go on to elaborate on Daly's earlier reveal to ABC Sport, saying Fagan had told them to use Wharfie Time against the Dockers, energising their own game instead.

"We talked about Wharfie Time and making that our energy [before the game]," Lions midfielder Josh Dunkley said.

"When I looked around at centre bounce and Wharfie Time came on, we all looked at each other, and connected, grew a leg and got it done.

"It's unbelievable."

Other players would say they felt the Dockers thought they had it won, and that you could feel the energy immediately rise in the Brisbane camp.

It was an inspired bit of coaching.

Will the Dockers use Wharfie Time again?

As ABC Sport writer Dean Bilton wrote in his analysis of the game, "it's cursed forever now, those bells now more likely to trigger an untimely bout of PTSD than to inspire the Freo faithful".

The Dockers have not confirmed or denied, and we may have to wait until the first close clash at Perth Stadium next year to know if Wharfie Time has been finally laid to rest.

title: Heritage buildings on cusp of ruin as stonemasons retire
text:
On a historic street near the southern tip of Western Australia, work is underway to restore a church that is more than a century old.

Constructed in 1892 with locally sourced granite and lime mortar, the fine craftsmanship of the heritage-listed building is characteristic of Australia's colonial era.

But with many heritage stonemasons on the cusp of retirement, structures like these will crumble if a new generation is not trained in the dying craft.

Despite the advent of power tools, hand tools like chisels and mallets are still used for heritage restoration work. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Trade close to extinction

Duncan Moon immigrated to Australia from Wales in 1983 and has worked as a heritage stonemason for almost 40 years.

"Within a short time of arriving, I was on my first heritage restoration project, which was the old jail in Mount Barker," he said.

Mr Moon is close to retirement, but hesitant to put down his tools.

"I don't think I'm going to be able to retire because my phone keeps ringing," he said.

"There's a bit of a dearth of heritage stonemasons.

"I'd like to see them with my level of skill, and know that when I do retire and I'm finally put out to pasture that this younger generation have the thirst and the hunger for the job."

Duncan Moon has worked as a stonemason for more than 40 years. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

He said Albany's Scots Church was one of many heritage-listed buildings in Australia in need of restoration.

"The work on old buildings tends to be ongoing. Just about everywhere has done quite a lot of damage to their built heritage, either deliberately or inadvertently," Mr Moon said.

"Sometimes the work is undertaken incorrectly — a very sound knowledge of material and technique is required."

Heritage stonemasons need to be skilled in mouldings to repair ornamental building features, as well as tuck-pointing, a technique used to repair and replace crumbling mortar between stone.

Lime mortar, shipped from across the King George Sound, was used on early Albany buildings. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Pillars of history

There are more than 100,000 heritage-listed buildings in Australia, which Albany historian Malcolm Traill says are a vital part of the nation's past.

"You can look at society, and how it's evolved and changed, through the eyes of buildings," he said.

"See how people lived, what size buildings they were, what scale, their changes of use."

Malcolm Trail says heritage buildings are a vital part of Australia's history. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

He has warned without an urgent uptake in heritage trades, history will be left to crumble.

"These buildings, which are well over 100 years old, are only here because they are maintained," he said.

"If they're looked after they will survive, but if they're not they will decay and deteriorate.

"Once the building fails, it's going to be very expensive to actually bring it back to its original circumstance."

Traditional stonemasonry tools are handcrafted by Duncan Moon. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Training deficit

About 5,000 people are employed as regular stonemasons in Australia, with even fewer having the skills to work on heritage buildings.

It is a gap the Heritage Skills Association is racing against an aging workforce to fill.

Historic pub for sale This historic pub survived riots and an earthquake and has now been listed for sale.

"Except for your Cert III in South Australia in heritage skills trades, there's no other certification," chief executive Yolanda Cool said.

"As a group, we're now pushing for a project-based intergenerational model.

" We need to have formal training. "

Yolanda Cool says more formal training is needed to keep heritage trades alive. (ABC South West: Neve Brissenden)

She said more traditional trade courses were an essential step in preserving Australian history.

"If we're looking at heritage-listed buildings, including the National Trust Register at a state level, there's almost 20,000 buildings [in WA]," Ms Cool said.

"For many, it's cheaper to demolish and replace with modern materials than to repair, because they haven't got the skills."

Next generation

Heritage stonemason Evan Zlnay started his career at TAFE before taking up a specialised restoration apprenticeship.

He works for Colgan Industries, which employs only a few people under 30 but is trying to train younger workers.

"It's just been having the old boys show me the little tips and tricks of heritage work," Mr Zlnay said.

"You've got to do what they did in the old days.

"To learn, it takes a bit of time."

Evan Zlnay says more awareness is needed to help get more young people into the heritage trade. (Supplied: Evan Zlnay)

Mr Zlnay, who is in his 20s, says there needed to be more awareness about the trade.

"It's good because we go and fix up old things that you don't want to fall over, and make them look new again," he said.

"Not many people would know that it's an option.

"Everyone these days wants to be a plumber or a sparky."

Mr Zlnay said he had the opportunity to work on buildings across Western Australia, including at the world-class tourist attraction Rottnest Island.

"You get to work on the coolest places," he said.

"You get satisfaction out of your job because you fix an old building and make it look new, but also not new at the same time."

title: Darwin teen 'in shock' after being selected to play in FIFA under-15 World Cup
text:
Long before Mark O'Connor ever thought about donning the green-and-gold jersey, there was football in the streets of Darwin.

Back then, the now 15-year-old was just like any other kid playing kickabouts with his mates when his father signed him up to a local club.

He could not have imagined it would be the first step towards representing his country.

Mark has since played for local clubs Greater Palmerston United (GPU), Mindil Aces and Darwin Olympic and now is preparing to join Australia's U-15 FIFA World Cup squad in Baku, Azerbaijan next month.

Mark O'Connor says he never imagined he would be selected to represent Australia in soccer. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I'd say [I was] almost in shock, in disbelief, because I didn't expect any of this to happen," he says.

" And then I felt super excited, but also kind of in disbelief. "

For a Northern Territory teenager who never thought standing on the world stage was something that happened to kids from the Top End, the moment means everything.

"Ever since I was playing from a young age, this is the type of thing that I'd want to be selected for," he says.

Mark O'Connor has played for three local soccer clubs in Darwin including Darwin Olympic. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Raw Territory talent

Mark's success was built through Darwin's footballing community, with different clubs playing a crucial role in his development.

Darwin Olympic president Yianni Prouzos says Mark's selection is also recognition of the region's talent.

"Mark started off as a GPU player, then he had a few years at Mindil Aces, and he spent a fair bit of time at Darwin Olympic," he says.

"For the size of the population, I believe there is a lot of raw talent in the Northern Territory."

Yianni Prouzos says there is a lot of young talent in Darwin's local soccer scene. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Even so, Mr Prouzos says Mark stood out, and he still remembers the first time he saw the marauding midfielder whose inspiration is Premier League giant, Liverpool's Steven Gerrard, play the game.

"The first time he took the pitch, the way he moved with the ball, change of direction of the body, amazing scanning," he says.

"Very small body, a lot of people target him, [but] he gets up.

"His determination, he keeps on coming back and back."

Mark O'Connor has been praised for his skill and determination. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The underdog

Mark says playing football in the tropics, where travelling down south for tournaments often means arriving as the underdog, prepared him for the challenge ahead of facing some of the best young footballers in the world.

"The NT would never really, I'd say, do very well down south, so being the underdog a lot was quite challenging," he said.

"To play against some of the best junior players in the world, it's really special to me.

Mark O'Connor says his previous experience competing interstate has helped prepare him for the international games. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I can see the levels that they're at and see how I compare to them as well."

Darwin Olympic teammate Anthony Reichstein says Mark's selection gives other Territory players something to aspire to.

"I think it gives a lot of the boys and girls up here a chance to make it now because they're clearly looking at Darwin now and it gives everyone a lot of hope," he says.

Beyond Darwin

Football Australia selected players from all nine of its member federations, with young footballers from metropolitan and regional areas earning a place in the national squad.

Talent identification lead Michael Cooper says that representation is particularly important for regional players.

"When you're in these regional areas, you do need that role model," he said.

"You do need to know that pathway is alive for you."

Michael Cooper says the opportunity to play for Australia is particularly important for regional players and their families. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

For Mark, the message is one he knows from experience.

"I started out at the same level as everyone else, playing for the same clubs in the NT," he said.

"And you can really make it to any level you want through enough hard work and dedication."

The gold knee-high boots Kylie Minogue spun around the MCG in on Saturday afternoon could outshine her iconic gold hot pants in the fashion stakes after one of the most memorable AFL grand final performances of all time. Though Minogue wore three custom outfits from Dolce & Gabbana during her celebrated pre-game performance, it was her choice of boots from the Melbourne label Bared Footwear that we can’t get out of our heads. Kylie Minogue wears Dolce & Gabbana with Bared Footwear’s knee-high boots to perform at the grand final. Eddie Jim Like her clothing choices, Minogue’s boots were custom-made. Bared founder Anna Baird travelled to her factory in China and personally brought them back for the big event. When the grand final performance was announced, Baird, who founded the footwear label 18 years ago, contacted Minogue’s stylist, Frank Strachan, to see if they could work with the Grammy winner.

Advertisement

“She was really happy to be in an Australian brand,” Baird said. “We ended up getting her seven different pairs and I brought them back myself from the factory.” Another reason for the customer order: Minogue’s special specifications. “She’s got tiny feet … She actually ended up in a size 34, which is our smallest size,” Baird said. Anna Baird of Melbourne brand Bared with a pair of Minogue’s custom-made grand final boots. Luis Enrique Ascui Ultimately, Minogue opted for three pairs of Bared boots on game day, as well as a lower pair for rehearsals. The shoes had to be able to not only withstand rainy weather, but also hold firm as Kylie shimmied her way around the stage. “She’s so iconic,” Baird said. “It was pretty awesome seeing her up there, and the shoes stood out so much.”

Advertisement

The 58-year-old star is one of a handful of A-list entertainers who have worn the label’s shoes recently. Meryl Streep and BlackPink popstar Jennie Kim are among fans of the brand. “It’s quite cool that all these people are actually wanting to perform and be comfortable in shoes,” Baird said. “It makes a massive difference rather than teetering around in stilettos.” Loading Though Baird said the true test of success was if a celebrity asked for another pair, Minogue is now well stocked with seven pairs. A trained podiatrist, Baird created the brand to fill what she saw as a gap in the market for shoes that were comfortable and wearable, but also stylish.

Advertisement

Anna Baird on her way back to Australia from China with Minogue’s boots. “Now we are very much a fashion brand that makes shoes that are comfortable, and I think the desirability is very much there,” she said. Minogue opened her performance in a Dolce & Gabbana cotton mesh tank top embellished with her name, a belt hung with red, white and black ribbons and Swarovski crystals, fishnet stockings and knee-high Bared boots in black. She then changed into a mini-dress made from a vintage jersey T-shirt with lace-up details and the word “Melbourne” in gold lettering on the back, donned the gold knee-high boots and launched into the unmistakeable sounds of her dance floor anthem Spinnin’ Around. To close the performance, Minogue emerged from a giant Sherrin football and soared above the crowd wearing a chiffon and chantilly lace gown with crystal mesh details – and opted for another pair of black boots.

Over the years, Kylie has used fashion to anchor each era as a pop chameleon, and told Vogue Australia her grand final outfits were carefully considered. “Performing in the round at the MCG means every piece had to work from every angle and speak to the 100,000 [people] in the audience – as well as everyone tuned in at home,” she said. “All the looks are playful nods to signature looks that mean a lot to us, while also tying in the football theme.” Baird is thrilled that Minogue has brought her shoes to a new audience, and hopes the gold boots will achieve the same cult status as Kylie’s gold hot pants – which are housed in the Australian Performing Arts Collection at the Arts Centre and rumoured to be worth $10 million. “Hopefully people will remember these boots in 20 years when they look back on her grand final performance” Baird said. “That is pretty cool.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: ‘I thought I was dreaming’: The Australian brothers turning football jerseys into high fashion
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Their boxy, vibrant silhouettes were once the domain of diehard fans fuelled by fond memories of beer-soaked nights in cacophonous suburban stadiums in the 1990s. Today, retro football jerseys are a hot fashion item, highly sought after by both women and men flaunting them in hip bars, on runways, and across social media feeds. It’s a craze fuelling a boom for Australian shirt dealers, while globally, the trend has attracted private equity dollars, pushing some vintage kit businesses toward $100 million valuations. Surging demand stems from a broader appetite for nostalgia in fashion and a desire to express belonging, experts say. But this thriving secondhand ecosystem operates distinct from the multi-billion-dollar industry that fuels the shirts’ initial creation. A display of Adidas reissued historical football jerseys at their headquarters in Germany in March this year. Adidas recently lost its long-held rights to manufacture the German national team’s shirts. Bloomberg For decades, sportswear giants have paid astronomical licensing fees to produce a team’s merchandise line – Nike, for example, currently pays European giant FC Barcelona FC a reported €127 million ($206 million) per season – with clubs receiving only a slim cut of each new shirt sold to fans. Modern shirts tend to retail for about $130 each, with extra fees to put a specific player’s name and number on the back. But while official replicas fund modern football, the second-hand trade has exploded from a niche fan community into a multi-million-dollar global market.

Advertisement

Related Article NRL 2025 Explaining Australia’s enduring love affair with vintage sportswear Retro shirts retail anywhere from $100 up to $500 depending on rarity and era, while iconic match-worn jersey can fetch millions at auctions. The shirt that Argentina great Diego Maradona wore when he scored the infamous “hand of God” goal against England in the 1986 world cup set a record when it sold for £7.14 million ($13.5 million) at auction in 2022. Several factors have driven this sport-fashion crossover, says Emily Brayshaw, a lecturer in fashion and design history at the University of Technology Sydney. She points to a desire for quality over fast fashion, the rise of athleisure, and blurred gender lines. “They’re incredibly comfortable, breathable, and you can dress them up,” she says. “If [men] don’t want to be seen as too feminine, you can still wear a pink or mint shirt, and because they’re associated with football, there’s a masculine element.” Pop star Dua Lipa posting a photo of herself wearing a Napoli jersey to social media. Dua Lipa/Instagram Brayshaw adds that the oversized, colourful designs of the 1990s offer an edge in a mainstream fashion landscape that has gone beige. Nostalgia for bygone sponsors and old fonts adds aesthetic appeal, tying into the current early-2000s Y2K revival playing out and the marriage of football and style spearheaded by David Beckham. For football supporters, it can mean connecting with their team’s heritage. For others, retro jerseys can be a way to engage with nostalgia for a bygone era, Brayshaw says. “They’re a window into the past.”

Advertisement

These dynamics are clear online. A recent Pinterest summer trend report finds that “football shirts take the lead as the hero top,” with searches for how to style national team shirts surging by up to 840 per cent. Images of celebrities like Kim Kardashian and Dua Lipa wearing retro jerseys have propelled the shirts into the mainstream. The jersey phenomenon is so advanced that even band and restaurant merch is now being released in the style of collared football shirts, with logos in place of a club crest. English Premier League club Arsenal is one of many teams to reissue a retro jersey from the 1990s due to soaring demand, about 30 years after they were first released. Arsenal Football Club But there’s nothing like the real thing. Fashion resale apps like Depop have reported a 77 per cent spike in jersey searches between 2024 and 2026, while eBay has recorded a similar jump for vintage Socceroos and AFL gear. “Football brings people together and gives us a chance to proudly support that community,” says Peter Freestone, eBay’s director of categories. Paul Blake, a self-described football romantic, launched retro shirt retailer PFC Vintage in 2019 and has seen it boom into a physical shop, fuelled partly by the ‘blokecore’ trend. “I’m not a fashion-forward guy, I got into this because I’m a football fan, but we’ve stumbled into the fashion space now, and we’ve seen that these customers are willing to spend,” he says. Clubs now release a new home, away and third kit every year, which Blake believes can exhaust fans.

Advertisement

A merchandise collaboration between Australian band DMAs and A-League club Sydney FC, modelled by player Rhyan Grant in the style of a retro football jersey – despite both the band and team being founded years after the style of shirt was first introduced. DMAs/Instagram Blake must painstakingly hunt down all of this stock. To manage the risk of ending up with stock that won’t sell, he focuses on kits from the 1980s, 90s, and 2000s – the aesthetic he believes is the current “sweet spot” for both diehard fans and fashion buyers. “It’s supply and demand, and the demand is very much here right now. But supply is limited, there’s no manufacturer to order from,” he says. To capitalise on this shortfall, clubs and manufacturers such as Nike and Adidas are now re-issuing popular heritage shirts, a trend seen locally with sold-out heritage NRL jerseys and Australian-made vintage AFL wool guernseys. Socceroo Jackson Irvine wearing a retro Japan jersey in a picture he posted to social media. Jackson Irvine/Instagram International dealer Classic Football Shirts is perhaps the industry biggest player, growing from a Manchester student dorm online operation in 2006 into a global powerhouse with physical stores in the UK and US. In May 2024, American the private equity firm Chernin Group took a minority stake in the company with a £30.4 million growth equity investment. Analysts have valued the business at approaching £50 million ($94 million). Back home, Brisbane start-up Unwanted FC is turning heads around the globe with its very different approach. While they collect and sell vintage shirts, its founders, twins Kevin and Keith Chan, were inspired to upcycle unused or damaged kits after seeing the football industry’s wastage firsthand as interns at Adidas’s headquarters in Germany.

Advertisement

“Our jobs as interns were to destroy samples, we couldn’t even donate them,” says Kevin. They spoke about the conundrum with their aunt, a retired tailor, who helped them turn an old kit into a tote bag. Founders of Unwanted FC Kevin and Keith Chan at their new Sydney store. Steven Siewert After launching in 2018, their business has grown to upcycle kits into boot bags, toiletry kits, hats, women’s crop tops and shirts with shirring, and now, business shirts and ties. They recently opened a concept store in Sydney. Manipulating the stretchy fabric is tricky, requiring several experienced garment technicians to sew the designs together. The Matildas’ popularity has generated immense interest from women looking to signal their affection for the game with unique items. Players including Ellie Carpenter modelling their upcycled garments on Instagram has boosted this and about half of Unwanted FC’s customers are now women, the brothers say. “They think they can get more use out of a side bag or a tote bag than a jersey ... it’s a different way to wear, it’s [more] accessible.” But altering jerseys can come at an emotional cost. At one point, the brothers pleaded with a customer who had sent in a rare 90s Arsenal sweatshirt to reconsider their request for it to be chopped up. “We just couldn’t cut it up, so instead of taking her money, we bought it off her,” says Kevin. Their work has caught the eye of global football royalty. Kevin recalls the moment he saw Spanish footballer and fashion icon Hector Bellerin photographed holding one of Unwanted FC’s reworked items. “I couldn’t sleep that night, I literally thought I was dreaming,” he says.

title: Locals are not lovin’ plans for new McDonald’s outlets in these tourism towns
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaHealth Locals are not lovin’ plans for new McDonald’s outlets in these tourism towns Benjamin Preiss September 27, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Phillip Island residents started looking for details about a new McDonald’s outlet proposed for the township of Cowes, their online searches generated some confounding results. Why were there so many responses about a fast food application in England’s Isle of Wight? An artist’s impression of the proposed McDonald’s store in Cowes. The communities of Cowes on Phillip Island and the town of the same name on the Isle of Wight are separated by more than 17,000 kilometres, but share a common fear about their future. In both coastal communities, there has been a fierce backlash against plans for a new McDonald’s outlet. Those concerns, however, are not limited to Cowes. Across Victoria, from Castlemaine to Northcote, residents are fighting the fast food giant’s encroachment.

Advertisement

Many Phillip Island residents who oppose McDonald’s plans want the Bass Coast Shire to follow the lead of its British counterpart and reject the application for a 24-hour outlet. Say No to McDonald’s member Trevor Ryan said community concerns about the proposed outlet for Cowes ranged from environmental damage and health impacts to traffic and road safety issues – particularly for young children at the primary school just metres away. Opponents of the proposed McDonald’s outlet for Phillip Island fear fast food will bring litter that will be damaging for wildlife. Joe Armao He said the global hamburger chain would devastate the tourism destination’s food scene by taking business away from local operators. “Phillip Island’s appeal is built around distinctive local food, drink and visitor experiences,” Ryan said.

Advertisement

Related Article Diet Town and country: The bunfight over McDonald’s in two very different locations Opponents fighting McDonald’s in Cowes fear it will generate a wave of packaging litter that will compromise Phillip Island’s unique coastal wildlife. “Rubbish does not just blow into the next suburb, it blows into our ocean,” Ryan said. McDonald’s has applied to the Bass Coast Shire to operate 24/7 with a maximum of 50 seats. If approved, the outlet would be less than 20 metres from the boundary of Cowes Primary School and is directly opposite retirement home units. It would be the first McDonald’s outlet on Phillip Island. The application has triggered about 1000 objections lodged with the Bass Coast Shire council. By comparison, it has received 26 letters in support.

Advertisement

One of those supporting letters said a McDonald’s outlet would provide jobs for young people as well as somewhere to get coffee after 2pm and food after 8pm when other businesses have closed. Another supporting letter said the proposed site was beside a service station, making it a suitable location while also providing a food choice for emergency services and shift workers. A 7-Eleven outlet has been approved for that service station site. Geoff Moed and Trevor Ryan on the site of the proposed McDonald’s outlet in Cowes. Justin McManus However, an online petition opposing the McDonald’s outlet in Cowes has more than 5700 signatures. Cowes health and wellness coach Victoria McGregor-Dawson said Phillip Island did not need McDonald’s. She said the location directly opposite retirement units was particularly problematic.

Advertisement

“You’ve got the elderly people living here, and they’re going to be infringed upon by lights, noise, smell on every level,” she said. Later this month, the Bass Coast Shire will hold a public meeting to hear from residents about their views on the proposed McDonald’s outlet. Victoria McGregor-Dawson says there are few redeeming qualities for McDonald’s in Cowes. Justin McManus But councils have traditionally had little power to reject fast food planning applications. And when they do, the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal can overturn those decisions. A McDonald’s outlet is under construction in Northcote despite vehement protests from residents. The Victorian parliament has passed legislation giving councils new powers enabling them to consider the health implications of planning applications. Presently, councils cannot assess planning applications on health grounds.

Advertisement

title: Flood disaster declared in Bangkok after more than 300mm falls in monsoon deluge
text:
Key Points More than 300mm of rain has fallen on Bangkok in 48 hours, causing flood across the city.

A flood disaster was declared across the city, and the prime minister cut short a trip to London.

Bangkok authorities declared a flood disaster across the Thai capital on Saturday after almost 48 hours of heavy rain left homes, shops and roads waterlogged and residents wading through waist-deep water.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul cut short a trip to London to return home after more than 300mm of rain fell in some areas between Thursday afternoon and Saturday morning, according to officials.

"The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now," said Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, a vendor who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok.

"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now," she told AFP.

Bangkok is no stranger to wet weather, and September is the peak of the rainy season, but several residents said it felt worse than usual.

"I feel like in all the many years I've lived here, I've never encountered anything like this, where it rains continuously for days," said 63-year-old resident Anutin Meechamnan.

The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) declared a disaster across all 50 districts of the city, a move that grants local organisations special powers to act.

Bangkok governor Chadchart Sittipunt said on Saturday afternoon that the situation had "stabilised", adding: "If more rainwater doesn't fall in the area, it will be solved."

"If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take two to three days to drain the floodwater," he said in an update broadcast on social media.

Temporary shelters

Almost continuous rain since Thursday afternoon has swelled Bangkok's network of canals, sending murky water into surrounding homes, restaurants, shops and alleyways.

"Our problem is that the canals are full," Chadchart said.

"We are cooperating with nearby provinces and try to drain water out through other sides, minimising the amount that flows into Bangkok."

Bangkok is built on former marshland and rests about 1.5 metres above sea level.

The BMA said earlier that the city's pumping stations were operating at full capacity, drawing a combined 1,200 cubic metres per second.

AFP reporters saw residents wading or pushing their motorcycles through high waters in several districts of eastern Bangkok, while parked cars were partially submerged on one major road.

In Bang Bua district, a woman tried to salvage goods from her shop as the floodwaters rose to her thighs.

Khem Amnueilaph, an office worker who lives in Suan Luang district in eastern Bangkok, said the water in his neighbourhood was "higher than knee level".

"My house is new so it was elevated, but some old houses nearby the water have already flooded," the 36-year-old told AFP by telephone.

"I have food in my stock for two to three days, but I may have to wade through the floodwater for food later," he said, adding: "I have no idea how to get to work on Monday."

Some convenience stores were out of stock by lunchtime as residents raced to buy essentials.

Chadchart said at least 13 major roads were flooded but urged residents not to worry about potential food shortages, stressing: "The public doesn't have to be panicked."

He said around 980 people were staying in temporary shelters, while authorities had transferred 36 bedridden people to hospitals. The city has also prepared one million sandbags.

Despite hopes that the water will recede, Bangkok authorities said schools would close on Monday, while some officials have been asked to work from home.

September has been wetter than usual, according to figures from Bangkok's drainage and sewerage department.

The capital recorded 487mm of rain between 1 and 25 September compared to an average of almost 269mm for the same period from 1991 to 2020.

Scientists warn the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to warm due to fossil fuel emissions.

Flooding was also reported on Saturday across 21 provinces in Thailand, according to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation, with more rain expected on Sunday.

Widespread deluges across the country in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.

title: Migrants are sending billions overseas. What does it mean for Australia's economy?
text:
In brief Remittances have become a contentious point in Australia's migration debate.

Critics argue they drain the Australian economy, while proponents say the provide a crucial lifeline to family abroad.

Remittances have become a talking point in Australia's migration debate.

Some anti-immigration activists argue remittances drain money from the Australian economy, while others say that view ignores migrants' economic contribution and the support these payments provide to families overseas.

So what's the real impact — both for the economy and for migrants and their families?

Mrinaal Datt, who moved to Australia from India four years ago and is the founder of Indian Women Abroad, regularly sends money back to India — often a few hundred dollars at a time.

She told SBS Examines that the remittances went towards her partner's parents' medical expenses.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"In Indian and a lot of South Asian cultures in general, they have a saying that you don't just marry a person, you marry the whole family," she said.

"It's not just you and your partner. It's your siblings, your parents, their parents. You can't think of not supporting your family. It's just not comprehensible to an average person who comes from India.

"It just feels like it's your duty as a child to support them through all their medical procedures."

A Money Transfer Australia report said $35 billion was sent from Australia as remittances in 2024, including nearly $7 billion to India.

"When someone earns that money in Australia, but remits part of that portion overseas, that portion is not being spent here," political commentator Jaimie Johnstone said in a recent social media post about the report.

"That money is not going to an Australian cafe or restaurant. It's not being spent with an Australian tradie, it's not being used to purchase Australian products, not in an Australian shop, not circulating within an Australian household.

"And if we're going to have a serious national conversation about immigration, surely capital flowing out of our domestic economy should be part of that conversation too."

But Ryan Edwards, an associate economics professor at the Australian National University, says we should be sceptical of these numbers.

"We don’t really measure money going out very well ... those numbers are actually much softer," he said.

Even if those estimates were correct, "that would still be under 1 per cent of our economy" and tax had already been paid on the income.

He noted the argument against remittances didn't account for the benefits migrants bring.

"The real counterfactual here is one of a migrant versus no migrant," he said.

"You take away that person, yes, you've stopped the money from flowing out, but you've also stopped all the jobs, the wages that they spend here, often on things that Australians are producing, and the tax that they've paid.

"We know that most migrants tend to be net positive fiscal contributors."

Muhammad Omair Ziaee is a technology and healthcare entrepreneur of Pakistani heritage. He sends money to his family and employees back home in Pakistan, but he says most of the money his businesses make is spent in Australia.

"If we compare to the money which we're sending over ... that's under 20 per cent of what we actually earn and what we spend over here," he said.

Remittances part of culture

Supriya Singh, an adjunct sociology professor at La Trobe University, said money is "one of the foremost ways" to show care in many cultures.

"If you come from China, you come from Vietnam, you come from any part of the Middle East, you come from the Pacific; sending money home is a way you tell your family that you belong, that you're thinking of them, that you care for them."

She said care was expressed differently across cultures.

"Across the world, it's the people who do not send money home that are in the minority," she said.

However, Singh said remittances can be used as a tool for financial abuse, noting the issue came up during Victoria's Royal Commission into Family Violence.

"When a person is using them not for care but for appropriation. If the parents demand too much of the child and the child does not have enough money for his or her own settlement expenses, then remittances can become a medium of abuse," she said.

Strain on already tight budget

Datt from Indian Women Abroad said remittances are a cultural practice but can strain already tight budgets.

"I think parents have to realise is that your child is not your retirement plan," she said.

"Everyone who comes abroad knows that it is really really hard when you're paying for the university fee. So many people are living paycheque to paycheque. It really is like a cultural thing. I actually hope things will change for the next generation."

She added her contributions to Australia outweighed the remittances back home.

"If you think about all the money that we spent, the flights that we paid, the income tax that we pay, our rentals, our mortgage now, I think we've spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in Australia," she said.

"The $200 or $400 is sent back home. That's nothing in comparison."

According to a World Bank estimate, global remittances to low and middle-income countries reached $924 billion in 2023, and continued to be "essential drivers of economic and human development".

title: Jane Hume says 'we're missing the point' on OpenAI Medicare breach
text:
In brief Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has criticised the government's response to the OpenAI Medicare breach.

It comes after the government suggested taking legal action against the US-based ChatGPT developer over the incident.

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume has accused the federal government of "missing the point" in its response to the OpenAI Medicare breach, arguing the incident exposed serious gaps in Australia's cyber defences.

The government is examining whether those involved in the breach could be prosecuted under existing Australian law.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said a task force investigating the incident was seeking advice on what action was possible under current laws and whether changes were needed to deal with similar incidents in the future.

Speaking on ABC's Insiders on Sunday, Hume said the "real alarm bell" was that the government only became aware of the hack because OpenAI disclosed it.

"I'm not entirely sure who they're going to put into cuffs," she said. "I think we're missing the point here."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"If they hadn't of told us that there was a breach, would we have known about it at all? That demonstrates that our cyber defences, particularly for [Services Australia], was woefully inadequate."

She questioned whether OpenAI was at fault, adding, "the idea that we would only check an inbox once a day when that inbox is specifically set up to identify cybersecurity breaches is mind-boggling".

Her comments follow Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's revelation this week that an agent linked to OpenAI, the California-based developer of ChatGPT, gained unauthorised access to Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

Both the government and OpenAI have said no personal information was accessed during the breach, but it has raised broader concerns, including over the time it took to report it and who is accountable.

The 18 June incident was reported to Services Australia by OpenAI on 10 September, when the company emailed a Services Australia inbox.

Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said that inbox is typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems, and is only checked once a day.

She said the email was discovered the next day and escalated on 15 September after checks to determine it was legitimate.

She said she was notified on 17 September. Albanese disclosed it publicly on 24 September.

PM says incident was not isolated

There have been dozens of cases of artificial intelligence agents wrongfully accessing classified information beyond Australia's Medicare hack, Albanese said on Saturday.

But he said he wasn't aware of them before revealing the unauthorised OpenAI infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting portal while in New York on Thursday.

"At the time we made our announcement ... we weren't aware of other occurrences," the prime minister told reporters on the tarmac at Sydney airport.

"We were acting purely in our national interest."

Albanese returned to Australia after a week in the US, where he addressed the United Nations General Assembly on the international need to rein in AI.

He now says news that rogue AI agents hacked into US government websites is further proof of that need.

Autonomous agents are now known to have infiltrated US university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

"We now know it wasn't just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation," Albanese said.

"What this does is confirm that approach of making sure that it needs to be an appropriate national response, as well as an international response to make sure that humans are in charge of this new and emerging technology."

Albanese said it was up to OpenAI to state why multiple breaches occurred.

Albanese spoke with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman by phone while in New York, with the tech boss admitting the company had not done enough.

Australia is among more than 20 countries that signed a joint statement calling for cooperation to establish global AI standards and ensure human control.

However, US President Donald Trump used a speech at the UN to lash out at calls to put the brakes on AI.

When Emma's relationship ended, the financial uncertainty didn't.

She says her former partner's child support payments became inconsistent, leaving her struggling to rely on the money she was entitled to. It forced her to rethink how she could protect herself and her child.

"I couldn't rely on the payments coming through," Emma tells SBS News.

There were elements of domestic violence, emotional abuse and coercive control behaviours.
