SBS News has withheld her surname for privacy reasons.

In a bid to protect herself and her child, Emma switched to Agency Collect, the government's Child Support Scheme (CSS), where Services Australia collects payments on behalf of separated parents.

For 18 months, Emma was receiving the child support she was entitled to — until the payments stopped.

She says her former partner took advantage of a "loophole" in the system and registered themselves as "self-employed" to avoid paying the amount she says was owed.

As of March 2026, almost $2 billion in child support debt was owed by parents using Agency Collect.

As of March 2026, outstanding child support debt among parents using Agency Collect stood at almost $2 billion. Source: iStockphoto / Tolikoff Photography/Getty Images/iStockphoto

A Department of Social Services (DSS) spokesperson told SBS News: "The amount of unpaid child support in this country is utterly unacceptable ... This is parents robbing their children of the support they need and in many cases leaving them to live in poverty."

But that figure only captures debt recorded through Agency Collect. It does not include unpaid child support under private arrangements between parents, meaning the full scale of the problem is unknown.

Emma's experience raises questions about how Australia's child support system responds when payments stop and what happens when financial control continues after a relationship ends.

How Australia's Child Support Scheme works

The CSS was introduced in 1988. It was designed to create a national system for assessing and collecting child support, with the aim of ensuring separated parents contributed financially to the cost of raising their children.

The scheme initially relied heavily on compulsory collection, including through wage withholding, where child support could be deducted from a person's salary.

However, by the mid-1990s, the scheme was reformed, giving parents greater choice over how their child support was collected.

Professor Kay Cook is an associate dean of research at Swinburne University of Technology, who specialises in child support policy. She says the reforms reflected a view within the government at the time that the system was "too onerous" on fathers.

They gave parents more choice, and it was all done under the rhetoric of making it easier and fairer ... but it returned all the power to the fathers.

Cook argues the changes shifted greater responsibility for managing child support onto parents, while government policy at the time emphasised giving separated parents more choice and flexibility in how payments were arranged.

For separated parents, there are two main routes for child support payment.

The first is Private Collect, a personal agreement in which payments are handled by the two parents without Services Australia collecting or monitoring.

Child support can be handled privately between separated parents or collected and managed by Services Australia through Agency Collect. Source: Moment RF / krisanapong detraphiphat/Getty Images

The second is Agency Collect, which is organised and overseen by the government through Services Australia.

There are 1.2 million Australians who have a child support arrangement — with 590,300 actively using Agency Collect.

The $1.99 billion owed by parents using Agency Collect does not capture those with Private Collect arrangements.

SBS News understands there are currently 229,355 non-paying parents — and only 59.4 per cent of them have an active repayment arrangement.

"We have no idea what is happening in the other half," Cook says, referring to Private Collect arrangements.

She believes the amount would be much higher.

Does the debt signal a bigger issue?

The debt is a result of an "underpayment of the amount that is meant to be paid in child support", according to Cook.

She says it most commonly occurs when the paying parent declares they are self-employed or "choose to pay or not pay when they want".

"People manipulate how much they pay, through working cash-in-hand jobs, or keeping their own business," she says.

They make their taxable income look really small.

Cook says there are little to no repercussions, describing Services Australia as a "toothless tiger".

In 2025, the Commonwealth Ombudsman investigated complaints about Services Australia's response to withheld payments and what it described as the "weaponisation" of child support.

The investigation found that Services Australia was "not doing enough to identify and respond to financial abuse through the Child Support program" and lacked "policies, strategies and training to be able to proactively identify, monitor and respond to cases of financial abuse".

A 2025 Commonwealth Ombudsman investigation found Services Australia was not doing enough to identify and respond to financial abuse through the Child Support program. Source: Moment RF / Kseniya Ovchinnikova/Getty Images

These findings prompted an Australian National Audit Office audit of Services Australia's child support debt-recovery enforcement powers. The findings are scheduled to be tabled in November 2026.

It's estimated that almost 100,000 parents using Agency Collect have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family or domestic violence.

Cook says the CSS operates under "the assumption that parents are equally bargaining and making decisions".

"But, in family violence ... when a perpetrator can't physically control you anymore, the number one tool they have left is to financially control you."

Adrianne Walters, executive director of Women's Legal Services Australia, says the "deliberate nonpayment of child support is economic abuse".

"It takes food off the table, destabilises households, and it punishes children in order to control their mothers," she tells SBS News.

The body recently surveyed 540 separated mothers, finding that 80 per cent reported experiencing financial abuse via the CSS.

Walters says the body regularly witnesses "women exhausted by the process".

"Years of underpayment and mounting debts, and the stress of other legal processes while the child support system asks them to keep pursuing a person they might be frightened of. Many simply give up," she says.

While the child support system has provisions intended to protect people experiencing family and domestic violence, Cook says they fail to account for the nuances of financial abuse.

"You have to prove it, and the system knows what to do with physical abuse, but it's not very good at recognising coercive control and financial abuse," she says.

[The CSS] is compelling women to be tied administratively to their abuser for decades.

"Instead, lots of women are just going to Private Collect and aren't collecting anything."

Do the new reforms actually fix the problems?

In the 2026-27 federal budget, the government announced a landmark $182.6 million investment over four years to reform the CSS.

The reforms include removing the requirement for certain personal financial information to be automatically shared with the other parent, increasing discretionary powers to limit harassment and harm between parents, expanding wage withholding and introducing a new Collection Arrangement Guidance Tool for new parents entering the CSS.

The government will also "strengthen data sharing" between Services Australia and the Australian Taxation Office and "prosecute people who don't lodge their tax returns to avoid their child support responsibilities".

From 1 July 2027, the government plans to automate the issuing of Departure Prohibition Orders (DPOs), a legal tool used by authorities to prevent people with significant unpaid debts from leaving the country.

That will include automatically issuing DPOs to some parents with child support debt of at least $10,000 who have travelled overseas more than once in the previous two years.

"We believe that if you can afford an overseas trip, then you can afford your child support," a DSS spokesperson told SBS News in a statement.

In the 2025-26 financial year, 672 DPOs were issued, according to the government. It expects the reforms to result in an extra 3,000 DPOs being issued in the first year.

Reforms will be legislated "progressively, with the first tranche to be introduced in parliament in the coming weeks", the spokesperson said.

Cook says the changes are "underwhelming" but are the "beginning of system change".

Walters noted that while they're the "most significant action taken against systems abuse in recent history", they fall short and do not fully address the experiences of parents in Private Collect arrangements.

She hopes to see the changes implemented with the safety of victim-survivors as a priority, and stronger access to free, specialist legal support for women to navigate the system safely.

"We need action to stop perpetrators from forcing women into Private Collect arrangements — like making Agency Collect the default arrangement until certain safeguards are met," Walters says.

"These actions must be accompanied by stronger accountability for deliberate non-payment ... better options for reviewing and enforcing Private Collect arrangements, so non-payment doesn't disappear from view."

The child support system means Emma will remain financially connected to her ex-partner until their child is at least 18. Credit: Christopher Hopefitch/Getty Images

Like many parents using the CSS, Emma will remain connected to her ex-partner until their child is at least 18 years old.

Believing the insecurity of payments kept her in the "cycle of abuse", she's worked hard to no longer be reliant on child support.

It came with significant sacrifice.

Sometimes you might have to ask people, your family, for help. You have to cancel things for yourself that might help your mental health.

"You might have to find housing in a non-ideal area because it's all you can afford, and you might have to work and juggle more.

"It's just part of the sacrifices you make as a parent — you put your child first."

If you or someone you know is impacted by family and domestic violence, call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732, text 0458 737 732, or visit 1800RESPECT.org.au . In an emergency, call 000.

The Men's Referral Service , operated by No to Violence, can be contacted on 1300 766 491.

title: Brisbane lions win AFL Grand Final in nail-biting finish against Fremantle Dockers
text:
In brief The Brisbane Lions are the 2026 Grand Final winners.

A couple tied the knot outside the stadium ahead of the match.

Brisbane have become the third team this century to claim an AFL premiership three-peat after beating Fremantle by seven points in an all-time classic grand final.

Fremantle led by 17 late in the game and were on course for a maiden premiership when Brisbane burst to life and Logan Morris put the Lions in front with a minute left, then kicked the sealer.

In prevailing 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) in front of 100,023 fans at the MCG, the Lions join Hawthorn (2013-15) and the legendary Brisbane team of 2001-03 to win three premierships in a row this century.

Two final-quarter goals from Logan Morris sealed victory for the Lions.

The Dockers pulled the trigger on their "Wharfie Time'' crowd activation when Patrick Voss put them up by 17 points, before Brisbane reeled them in, delivering coach Chris Fagan a third premiership amid heavy speculation it was his final game at the helm.

Brisbane midfielder Will Ashcroft (31 disposals, nine clearances) and co-captains Harris Andrews and Josh Dunkley were fantastic, along with forward Charlie Cameron (three goals) and veteran Dayne Zorko.

Charlie Cameron kicked three goals in the Lions' third straight AFL flag.

Brisbane champion and former Docker Lachie Neale, who contentiously had his one-game striking ban overturned at the AFL appeals board on Thursday, was heavily booed by the Fremantle fans throughout.

Heavy rain on Saturday morning meant covers were on the ground before the pre-game entertainment, headlined by Kylie Minogue, but the weather cleared up ahead of the main event

They love each other — and they love the Fremantle Dockers

On AFL Grand Final day, a couple from Western Australia took their commitment to both to the next level, tying the knot outside the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) ahead of the 2026 AFL Grand Final match-up against the Brisbane Lions.

Matt Abbott, Danni Bloomfield and their celebrant — a close friend — were all smiles as they performed the ceremony, clad in purple Dockers scarves over their wedding attire.

"I love you, and I will always be in your corner. I promise to stand by you through every Dockers game," Bloomfield said during her vows.

"Go Freo!"

Bloomfield told ABC News they had planned to get married and then "walk straight in and go and watch them bring home the cup". She said she even ordered a purple dress, but it didn't arrive in time.

The couple flew to Melbourne from Karratha to watch their beloved Dockers face the Lions. Source: SBS News

The couple, who have been together for 15 years, had been planning to throw a surprise wedding at Bloomfield's 50th birthday party, but pivoted at the last minute when their team made the final.

Their celebrant Luke Lalor told the ABC he'd never done a wedding with 100,000 guests, and thought it was a "fantastic" idea that they were marrying "exactly where they want it".

Bloomfield and Abbott are among thousands of Dockers and Lions fans who have travelled to Melbourne for the big match.

Pop superstar Kylie Minogue dazzled in an upbeat pre-game show, belting out hits such as Can't Get You Out Of My Head, Spinning Around and Padam Padam.

How did Brisbane and Fremantle get here?

Fremantle beat Brisbane 103-78 when the sides last met at the Gabba in May, at one stage leading by 51 points.

Dockers Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss kicked four goals each, while Josh Treacy added three.

Freemantle finished the home-and-away season as minor premiers, while Brisbane secured a top-four finish.

Neither side took the direct route to the grand final, with both losing their qualifying finals before fighting their way back.

Brisbane lost its qualifying final to the Sydney Swans by 53 points, then recovered with victories over the Adelaide Crows and Hawthorn Hawks to reach their fourth consecutive grand final.

Fremantle suffered a 72-40 loss to Hawthorn before bouncing back with wins over the Geelong Cats and Sydney to book a place in the final.

Brisbane won three consecutive premierships from 2001 to 2003, while the Dockers have never taken home the cup since entering the league in 1995.

title: Donald Trump praises Xi Jinping as US visit wraps up, but little progress on key issues
text:
In brief Chinese President Xi Jinping has wrapped up a three-day visit to the US.

US President Donald Trump praised the visit but no agreements were reached on major issues.

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping drank tea at the White House and visited the National Archives on Friday local time, ending a three-day summit that showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs on a host of contentious issues.

Trump said "our farmers are going to be happy" as a result of the talks but did not provide details.

"America is very happy about this visit, and I'm sure China is very happy also," he said.

Xi said the US-China relationship had developed into a constructive one of "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity".

The summit between the world's two largest economies featured military flyovers, ceremonial tours and a state dinner, but left unresolved major differences over trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan and China's ties to Iran. Details of the limited trade agreements reached during the visit will be released on Monday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

One tangible outcome of the visit was that the US and China agreed to extend by two months a trade truce that was due to expire on 10 November, allowing more time to work on ‌a potentially bigger trade deal.

Greer told CNBC that the US has agreed with China to exempt some key goods from trade disputes, including exports to China of agricultural products and medical devices, and imports of consumer and non-sensitive goods.

Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism, citing increased market access for US farmers and ranchers, while both leaders identified AI as an area for dialogue.

"In some ways, the best thing that we accomplished in this visit is to continue the conversation," US ambassador to china David Perdue told Fox News on Friday, local time.

Trump announced in a social media post that he and Xi would meet twice more this year, in China in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum and in Miami in December at a G20 summit.

"Much has been, and will be, accomplished," Trump said.

National archives tour

After tea in the White House Red Room, Trump and Xi rode in limousines to the National Archives, where they reviewed the US Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

Asked about Iran, Trump said he and Xi had discussed it and that "I think we're going to do great," without elaborating. China has denied US allegations of helping Iran's leaders in the conflict launched by Trump in February.

Perdue said in an interview with CNBC on Friday that Trump reiterated to Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was "totally unacceptable" and received assurances that China would not do so.

Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Thursday that Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran.

China presses on Taiwan

A key issue for Xi was the status of Taiwan.

China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own, and Xi has long sought to persuade Trump to state publicly that the US opposes Taiwan's independence, rather than merely saying it does not support independence, which has been the US's formulation for decades.

He also wants the US to halt arms sales to the island.

Xi pressed Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the US would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence".

China's state news agency also reported that Xi "hopes the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing 'Taiwan independence'".

While the US, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, Washington is its most important international backer and is bound by US law to provide it with the means to defend itself.

The US's Asian allies were watching closely to see how Trump talked about Taiwan following Xi's visit. As of Friday afternoon, he had said nothing substantive.

After his May summit with Xi, Trump, whose administration in December approved a US$11 billion ($15.6 billion) arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14 billion, in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip".

On Thursday, Democrats criticised Trump for failing to publicly address China's military pressure on Taiwan and called for the immediate delivery of approved military aid and arms sales to the island.

title: ‘Comprehensively bad thing to do’: Why we should stop putting data online
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Hacking attacks have become so common that keeping data safe feels like an impossible task, with some cybersecurity experts saying the system is "fundamentally broken".

Mihai Lazarescu worked for years as a 'white hat' hacker finding vulnerabilities in computer systems, and says organisations simply don't have the resources to effectively manage the threats.

The cyber security consultant, who is an associate professor at Curtin University, says news this week that Australia's Medicare statistics portal was hacked — the first known hack of an Australian government website by an agentic AI agent — is another example of the challenges involved in keeping data secure online.

While no personal information was believed to have been accessed, it follows major data breaches involving businesses including Origin Energy, Optus and Medibank in recent years, in which personal data was accessed or stolen.

"My experience dealing with different organisations — ranging from small businesses to banks — is that they struggle to find enough resources to cover [cyber security]," Lazarescu tells SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Even if they have the funds to protect their systems, finding people with the right skills is difficult.

The reality is that if people want to get to your data [and] it is available, they'll probably find a way to do it.

Lazarescu says continuing to place data online at the same rate "makes no sense" and the system is "fundamentally broken".

"We can't protect things, and now you have this emergence of automatic agents, why do we keep going it?"

Lazarescu says consumers need to push for change.

"If there's no pushback, this is going to keep going."

Should we go back to paper records?

In recent years, there's been a trend towards putting everything online, but given the security risks, Lazarescu questions why it's necessary for businesses, especially telcos and power companies providing essential services, to store their customer data on the internet.

These businesses have millions of customers, which means a cybersecurity breach has the potential to impact significant numbers of people.

Almost 10 million people had personal information accessed in 2022 when Optus' system was hacked, and around 10,000 had their data published on the dark web.

Customer data of mobile phone service provide Optus was compromised after a cyber attack in 2022. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

The hack of Origin Energy in July impacted almost one million current and former customers.

The number of hacking attacks is rising, with the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner saying it received 1,205 data breach notifications in 2025, an increase of 8 per cent from the previous year.

Until a system is developed that enables information to be stored securely, Lazarescu says some businesses should consider returning to paper records, something that was functional in the past.

I've seen all kind of benefits being touted [to putting stuff online]. I haven’t seen yet any evidence that [it's] paying off.

Lazarescu points out the internet is essentially "unsecurable", arguing its underlying protocols were designed in an era when computers were primarily being used to link academics at different universities and assumed users were trustworthy.

"At the fundamental level [it] can't be secured unless we have an internet 2.0, and I can’t see anybody trying to do that," he says.

This makes putting stuff online a "comprehensively bad thing to do".

But Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer at the School of Computer Sciences and Engineering at the University of New South Wales, is sceptical about whether returning to paper records is practical.

She says technology has advanced and a significant increase in printing could also increase carbon emissions.

"The only solution I can see is public awareness and sharing less data, and companies collecting less data," Masood tells SBS News.

Rethinking data collection

While companies should be minimising the amount of personal information they hold, they often have limited incentives to delete data once it has been collected. Masood says many companies earn money from selling data.

It’s now common for businesses to ask for personal details from customers even when some of that information may not be essential to providing the service.

Masood points to Medicare card details being stolen during the recent Quest Apartment Hotels data breach.

Why do you need the Medicare [details to rent an] apartment?

The Quest hack raises questions about not only what information businesses collect, but also how long they retain it. Some impacted customers told the media they had last interacted with the business years ago.

Masood says data should only be stored when it is needed, and then deleted after a certain time period, including when a person dies.

While fines of up to $2.5 million for a person, and up to $50 million or other substantial penalties for a company, depending on the circumstances, can be issued for privacy breaches in Australia, Masood points out that laws are often not enforced.

She believes companies operating in Australia should be audited to ensure they are meeting the requirements of the Privacy Act 1988. This regulates how government agencies as well as some organisations, including those with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, handle personal information.

Changes should also be made so that people are given user-friendly and concise information about companies' privacy policies, instead of pages of terms and conditions they don't understand.

Masood says customers need simple information about what type of data is stored on business servers, how it is used, why it is needed, the potential consequences of this data storage, as well as who they can contact with issues.

"It's not a difficult task, it's just that companies don't want to do it."

More accountability needed

Jacqueline Boaks, a lecturer at Curtin University who specialises in business ethics, says there's often a sense of inevitability around AI and a sense of powerlessness that anything can be done to stop it, but she argues that societies have well-established laws to hold people morally and legally responsible for creating and releasing a product that does harm.

"We shouldn't forget that, just because something's digital and not physical," she tells SBS News.

We as a community and as the government need to have an expectation morally and ethically around who is accountable and who is responsible when [hacks] happen.

Boaks says it's impossible for individuals to oversee how their data is managed by companies or to opt out of services such as Medicare.

"[This] is a pretty vulnerable place to be, but it does seem to be exactly the kind of thing that we have a right to expect governments to protect us from," she says.

"That's one of their core roles."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese indicated support for regulating artificial intelligence at an international level during a speech at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week. Source: AAP / Sarah Yenesel/EPA

But Boaks says there's often a disconnect between the level of harm done through these data leaks and the consequences faced by companies.

Lazarescu agrees the consequences are not serious enough for companies to change their practices.

What happens when you have a breach? Do you see anything in terms of people being held accountable? Organisations being held accountable?

Lazarescu, who grew up in Romania under Communist Party rule, is also sensitive to what could happen if more aspects of people's lives move into digital systems, particularly if governments can easily erase people.

"To me the biggest problem with putting stuff online is that you can also modify it online."

What can people do to protect their data?

Leaders such as United States President Donald Trump have rejected the need for stronger AI regulation, and Trump has also criticised Australia's plan for digital duty of care laws that would give residents the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds.

But Lazarescu says this doesn't mean every American agrees with the Trump administration's position.

People have a lot more power and they need to be engaged and tell the politicians enough is enough.

At an individual level, Lazarescu and Masood warn against sharing anything online unless it is absolutely necessary.

This includes posting on social media, which can allow companies to build detailed profiles of users, avoiding unnecessary sharing of documents such as passport copies, and not entering sensitive details into AI programs such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and other large language models.

"It's very crucial now," Masood says. "You need to be minimising the data yourself."

title: Extra cash for some Australians — and a card surcharge shake-up looms
text:
Major Australian companies are sending billions of dollars to shareholders’ bank accounts as dividend payment season ramps up.

BHP, which is Australia’s largest listed organisation, delivered US$5 billion ($7.12 billion) in dividends to its investors on Wednesday.

That means its 450,000 retail shareholders may have received a fully franked final dividend of $1.38 for each share they hold in BHP.

It’s been a big year for the so-called “Big Australian” after copper became the company’s largest earnings contributor for the first time.

The nation’s most widely held stock is Telstra, though, with an estimated 1 million shareholders.

On Thursday it delivered its final dividend of 10.5 cents per share, paying out $1.2 billion dollars over the last financial year.

Of course, not all shareholders elect to receive dividends into their bank account, with some opting to reinvest that payment instead.

Millions of Australians have exposure to shares like BHP and Telstra through their superannuation fund.

Credit and debit card surcharges are going

It might be worth paying closer attention at the checkout next week to see how businesses are handling new credit and debit card surcharge rules.

From 1 October, those surcharges will be banned, eliminating the fee that is added to the price of goods and services.

It means the advertised price of a product should be the price you pay at the checkout.

Right now, a $5 coffee, for example, might actually be $5.08 when a surcharge is applied.

While the RBA has reduced some background fees associated with card payments to help small businesses make the change, they’ll still incur an expense, which means many will be forced to decide whether to absorb it or pass it on to customers.

So, from 1 October, will that $5 coffee still be advertised as $5, or will it go up to $5.08 or more?

Sarah Megginson from consumer group Finder says some small businesses may look to other forms of payment to reduce costs.

“You can use PayID and bank transfers, which transfer instantly, so you might see small businesses turn to these more affordable ways to accept cash,” she told the SBS On the Money Podcast.

Some larger businesses are doing away with card payments altogether as a direct result of the changes.

DEFT, an online secure payment system used by thousands of renters and homeowners, no longer accepts debit or credit card payments, instead pointing customers to payment options like PayID, BPAY or Australia Post.

To fund the changes, banks are also making adjustments through rewards cards, annual fees and bonus points restructuring,

Not all fees and surcharges are disappearing with these new rules, though, because they don’t extend to weekend or public holiday surcharges, booking fees, or service fees.

Interest rates may still rise despite a higher jobless rate

Earlier this week, Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock warned the unemployment rate may need to rise to as much as 5 per cent to help ease inflation, which in turn could lower interest rates.

Fresh ABS data on Thursday revealed more people are now in the workforce or looking for work, which could be a sign of cost of living pressures, while of the near 40,000 jobs created last month, they were all part-time, suggesting many may have been related to Census workers.

The headline jobless rate has climbed from 4.5 per cent to 4.6 per cent, which is a near five-year high.

Westpac senior economist Pat Bustamante says the RBA is still likely to lift interest rates on Tuesday.

“We think a September hike is locked in and reflects the data we’ve already seen,” Bustamante said. “Going forward, particularly in November, if the labour market eases a bit more than what they’re expecting, we can see them pause and wait.”

Higher inflation will likely prompt the bank to pull the trigger, which is only likely to get worse, according to HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham, who has two more interest rate rises this year pencilled in.

Bloxham says this is because overseas factors are adding to inflation, like higher fuel prices from the Middle East war, unfavourable weather and El Niño driving up food prices, and the AI investment boom.

title: Last-minute Rayan equaliser denies Socceroos famous win against Brazil
text:
A last-minute header from Brazilian substitute Rayan salvaged a 1-1 draw with Australia in a thrilling international friendly in Townsville on Friday.

Rayan headed the ball home in the 95th minute to deny the hosts what would have been only their second win over the South American giants.

It was a fitting result from two evenly-matched teams who gave everything in front of a sell-out crowd in the North Queensland city.

A superb free kick from Nestory Irankunda had looked enough to give the Socceroos an upset win.

With the two sides locked at 0-0 midway through the second half, Irankunda stepped up and drilled his free kick over the defensive wall into the net, leaving Brazil keeper Hugo Souza rooted to the spot.

But Brazil came out and dominated against an increasingly defensive Australian outfit and were rewarded seconds before full-time.

With both teams looking to rebuild after early exits from this year's World Cup, the Socceroos seized the early advantage.

They dominated possession and territory, attacking with width and finding plenty of space on both sides.

Midfielder Connor Metcalfe went close in just the third minute before an Irankunda bullet forced a good save from Souza.

Brazil weathered the storm and began to find their rhythm, looking increasingly dangerous through in-form Barcelona striker Raphinha and Chelsea forward Estevao.

Raphinha had a good chance with a header straight to Australian keeper Patrick Beach after 20 minutes before Estevao forced a great save from Beach five minutes later.

The Brazil dominance appeared to have paid off in the 46th minute when Estevao scored, but a VAR review saw the goal ruled out due to an earlier foul on Australian captain Harry Soutar.

The second half saw much of the same, with Brazil controlling the centre and the Socceroos finding space out wide.

The visitors were just edging the match and it seemed only a matter of time before they scored, but they were shocked by Irankunda's superb free kick.

The Socceroos defended furiously and looked to have held out for the win, but a last-minute corner saw Rayan's header just too powerful for Beach to hold out.

title: Why Victoria may be millions of dollars better off with this AFL Grand Final match-up
text:
IN BRIEF Grand Final weekend could generate up to $75 million in economic activity for Victoria, according to one estimate.

But a sport business expert says the actual net benefit could be closer to $20 million to $25 million.

An all-interstate AFL Grand Final is expected to deliver a bigger economic boost to Victoria than a match between two Victorian teams.

Fremantle and Brisbane will meet at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in front an expected crowd of 100,000 people on Saturday in just the second all-interstate Grand Final since Victoria introduced its Grand Final Eve public holiday in 2015.

And tens of thousands of supporters travelling from Western Australia and Queensland are expected to pour money into Melbourne's hotels, restaurants, bars and other businesses.

RMIT University Professor Angel Zhong estimates Grand Final weekend could generate up to $75 million in economic activity for Victoria.

She says an all-Victorian derby could generate roughly a third of that figure because much of the money spent by local supporters would simply be redirected from elsewhere within the Victorian economy.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But Professor Hans Westerbeek, a sport business expert at Victoria University, says while the underlying argument is sound, the headline figure does not necessarily represent the amount Victoria ultimately gains.

"The Grand Final brings genuinely new money," he told SBS News.

But after accounting for money that leaves the state or economic activity displaced by the event, he estimates the real net benefit could be considerably lower.

So, where does the $75 million come from?

Zhong said the difference between an interstate and an all-Victorian Grand Final largely comes down to where supporters’ money originates.

"When interstate fans fly in, stay in hotels and eat in our restaurants, that is genuinely new money entering Victoria," she said in a statement.

"When people go to a local derby, they are mostly redirecting spending they would have made in the state anyway."

Westerbek agreed. Using what he described as a "back-of-the-envelope" calculation, Westerbeek compared a Grand Final in which about 90 per cent of spectators were Melbourne-based with one in which half the crowd travelled from interstate.

In the first scenario, he estimated roughly $5 million in value could be added to the Victorian economy.

READ MORE Suspended Swans players to make first public appearance since hotel scandal

If about half the crowd was interstate, he said that could rise to around $20 million to $25 million.

But, he said the gross visitor spend could be considerably higher.

Westerbeek estimated interstate visitors staying for two nights and spending on accommodation, food, drinks and tourism could generate around $60 million in visitor expenditure alone.

But emphasised that is not the same thing as Victoria being $60 million better off.

The money that doesn't make the headline figure

Westerbeek said headline economic impact figures can also be reduced by what economists call "displacement".

For example, some visitors who might otherwise have travelled to Melbourne could avoid Grand Final weekend because accommodation is booked out or more expensive, he said.

Their spending would therefore be replaced by that of visiting AFL fans, rather than representing entirely new economic activity.

That is separate from the substitution effect identified in RMIT's analysis, where spending by Victorian fans may simply be redirected from elsewhere in the state.

"There is definitely an influx of money, but there's also an outflow that is often not calculated in those headline figures," Westerbeek said.

READ MORE The numbers raising new questions about Australia's future wealth

Even money spent getting to Melbourne does not necessarily remain in Victoria.

Westerbeek said airfares, for example, largely go to airlines and travel operators that may be headquartered elsewhere.

What about Victoria's Grand Final public holiday?

For hospitality businesses packed with travelling football supporters, the public holiday the day before Saturday's big game can provide another day of strong trading.

But other businesses may face higher wage bills through public holiday penalty rates, fewer customers or an entire day without normal operations.

Zhong said whether the public holiday benefits a business depends heavily on its industry and location.

A restaurant near the MCG may have one of its strongest trading days of the year despite higher wage costs, while a business dependent on office workers could face higher costs and lower demand.

But a café reliant on office workers or a suburban restaurant with little connection to the game could face higher wage costs and fewer customers, or decide not to open at all.

Westerbeek said the wider loss of a normal working day was another factor that headline economic-impact estimates do not always capture.

For workers rostered on, penalty rates provide additional income.

But from a whole-of-economy perspective, Westerbeek said the lost productivity among sectors that shut down should also form part of any assessment of the weekend's financial impact.

"It certainly isn't something that is being featured or calculated when we talk about ... the headline reported benefits," he said.

That does not mean he believes Victoria loses from hosting the Grand Final.

"It is [a success]," he said.

"But it's not as substantial as the $75 million in terms of the headline number."

Melbourne's payoff goes beyond one weekend

Westerbeek told SBS News that the economic impact of the Grand Final is not limited to what visitors spend over the weekend, with Melbourne also deriving longer-term value from its reputation as a major events city.

Melbourne has spent decades positioning itself as a major-events city, with the AFL Grand Final sitting alongside events including the Australian Open and Formula One Australian Grand Prix.

Westerbeek said individual sporting events should therefore not necessarily be assessed in isolation.

"The AFL Grand Final is not a once-a-year kind of thing. It is part of a portfolio of events, a year-round calendar," he said.

Rather than suddenly transforming Melbourne's tourism economy each September, he said the Grand Final helps sustain the infrastructure, hospitality industry, expertise and reputation the city has built around major events.

"The Grand Final maintains Melbourne's reputation rather than building it," he said.

Evidence that a single event can create sustained tourism growth is relatively weak, Westerbeek said.

Melbourne's advantage is that the next major event is never particularly far away.

"It's not a peak moment," he said.

"It is a pulsating moment. It's one of many events that keep Melbourne, justifiably, as Australia's, maybe even one of the world's, major event and sports capitals."

The Australian Open tennis tournament is another big annual sporting event that draws visitors to Melbourne. Source: Getty / karenfoleyphotography

And while an interstate Grand Final may inject more outside money into Victoria, Westerbeek said the comparison misses something else entirely.

An all-Victorian Grand Final can generate social benefits for locals, including a sense of identity, pride and connection — that are difficult to attach a dollar figure to.

Those benefits may never appear in an economic-impact calculation.

But, he said, they are still part of what the Grand Final is worth.

title: 'Not a coincidence': Opposition questions timing of Albanese's OpenAI hack reveal
text:
In Brief James Paterson says the timing of the Medicare breach disclosure was politically motivated.

The government is examining whether OpenAI could face legal consequences over the breach.

The Opposition has questioned the timing of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's disclosure that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics portal, as pressure grows for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence.

Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he did not believe it was a "coincidence" that Albanese revealed the incident while attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

"The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did," Paterson told ABC's 7.30.

"I don't think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City."

Questions around timing of disclosure

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Paterson, however, played down the severity of the breach itself, describing it as being at the "bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness".

He said Australians should be "alert but not alarmed" about the incident, noting the information accessed was not personal or private Medicare data.

It reportedly occurred on 18 June when an OpenAI agent tasked with researching public medicine spending gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.

The government says the portal contained aggregated health statistics and was separate from systems handling Medicare claims or individual patient records.

READ MORE Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated

OpenAI detected the activity on 11 August but did not notify the Australian government until 10 September, when it sent an email to a Services Australia inbox.

Albanese publicly revealed the breach on Thursday after speaking with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman in New York.

The prime minister criticised both the length of time it took OpenAI to inform Australia and the way the notification was made.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he has spoken with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, "to express Australia's extreme concern". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Government examining legal options

The federal government has established a task force to investigate the incident, including whether Australia's existing laws and reporting requirements are adequate to deal with autonomous AI systems.

The review will also consider whether OpenAI breached Australian law and whether stronger penalties or liability rules are needed for companies whose AI agents cause harm.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Friday the government was examining what legal consequences could follow the incident, amid calls for OpenAI to be held accountable.

The government is also investigating whether activity linked to OpenAI agents affected systems belonging to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Victoria's Department of Health.

Calls for stronger AI safeguards

The breach has added to debate over how Australia regulates increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the incident demonstrated the need for stronger rules around transparency and incident reporting.

He told the ABC Australia could not be left "entirely at the mercy of foreign AI companies".

Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie also called for safeguards to ensure AI systems were fit for purpose, telling ABC Radio National Breakfast that Australia needed to make sure "AI serves humanity, not the other way around".

The government has said it plans to develop national AI standards, with findings from the investigation expected to inform its approach to future regulation.

title: ‘I thought I was dreaming’: The Australian brothers turning football jerseys into high fashion
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Their boxy, vibrant silhouettes were once the domain of diehard fans fuelled by fond memories of beer-soaked nights in cacophonous suburban stadiums in the 1990s. Today, retro football jerseys are a hot fashion item, highly sought after by both women and men flaunting them in hip bars, on runways, and across social media feeds. It’s a craze fuelling a boom for Australian shirt dealers, while globally, the trend has attracted private equity dollars, pushing some vintage kit businesses toward $100 million valuations. Surging demand stems from a broader appetite for nostalgia in fashion and a desire to express belonging, experts say. But this thriving secondhand ecosystem operates distinct from the multi-billion-dollar industry that fuels the shirts’ initial creation. A display of Adidas reissued historical football jerseys at their headquarters in Germany in March this year. Adidas recently lost its long-held rights to manufacture the German national team’s shirts. Bloomberg For decades, sportswear giants have paid astronomical licensing fees to produce a team’s merchandise line – Nike, for example, currently pays European giant FC Barcelona FC a reported €127 million ($206 million) per season – with clubs receiving only a slim cut of each new shirt sold to fans. Modern shirts tend to retail for about $130 each, with extra fees to put a specific player’s name and number on the back. But while official replicas fund modern football, the second-hand trade has exploded from a niche fan community into a multi-million-dollar global market.

Advertisement

Related Article NRL 2025 Explaining Australia’s enduring love affair with vintage sportswear Retro shirts retail anywhere from $100 up to $500 depending on rarity and era, while iconic match-worn jersey can fetch millions at auctions. The shirt that Argentina great Diego Maradona wore when he scored the infamous “hand of God” goal against England in the 1986 world cup set a record when it sold for £7.14 million ($13.5 million) at auction in 2022. Several factors have driven this sport-fashion crossover, says Emily Brayshaw, a lecturer in fashion and design history at the University of Technology Sydney. She points to a desire for quality over fast fashion, the rise of athleisure, and blurred gender lines. “They’re incredibly comfortable, breathable, and you can dress them up,” she says. “If [men] don’t want to be seen as too feminine, you can still wear a pink or mint shirt, and because they’re associated with football, there’s a masculine element.” Pop star Dua Lipa posting a photo of herself wearing a Napoli jersey to social media. Dua Lipa/Instagram Brayshaw adds that the oversized, colourful designs of the 1990s offer an edge in a mainstream fashion landscape that has gone beige. Nostalgia for bygone sponsors and old fonts adds aesthetic appeal, tying into the current early-2000s Y2K revival playing out and the marriage of football and style spearheaded by David Beckham. For football supporters, it can mean connecting with their team’s heritage. For others, retro jerseys can be a way to engage with nostalgia for a bygone era, Brayshaw says. “They’re a window into the past.”

Advertisement

These dynamics are clear online. A recent Pinterest summer trend report finds that “football shirts take the lead as the hero top,” with searches for how to style national team shirts surging by up to 840 per cent. Images of celebrities like Kim Kardashian and Dua Lipa wearing retro jerseys have propelled the shirts into the mainstream. The jersey phenomenon is so advanced that even band and restaurant merch is now being released in the style of collared football shirts, with logos in place of a club crest. English Premier League club Arsenal is one of many teams to reissue a retro jersey from the 1990s due to soaring demand, about 30 years after they were first released. Arsenal Football Club But there’s nothing like the real thing. Fashion resale apps like Depop have reported a 77 per cent spike in jersey searches between 2024 and 2026, while eBay has recorded a similar jump for vintage Socceroos and AFL gear. “Football brings people together and gives us a chance to proudly support that community,” says Peter Freestone, eBay’s director of categories. Paul Blake, a self-described football romantic, launched retro shirt retailer PFC Vintage in 2019 and has seen it boom into a physical shop, fuelled partly by the ‘blokecore’ trend. “I’m not a fashion-forward guy, I got into this because I’m a football fan, but we’ve stumbled into the fashion space now, and we’ve seen that these customers are willing to spend,” he says. Clubs now release a new home, away and third kit every year, which Blake believes can exhaust fans.

Advertisement

A merchandise collaboration between Australian band DMAs and A-League club Sydney FC, modelled by player Rhyan Grant in the style of a retro football jersey – despite both the band and team being founded years after the style of shirt was first introduced. DMAs/Instagram Blake must painstakingly hunt down all of this stock. To manage the risk of ending up with stock that won’t sell, he focuses on kits from the 1980s, 90s, and 2000s – the aesthetic he believes is the current “sweet spot” for both diehard fans and fashion buyers. “It’s supply and demand, and the demand is very much here right now. But supply is limited, there’s no manufacturer to order from,” he says. To capitalise on this shortfall, clubs and manufacturers such as Nike and Adidas are now re-issuing popular heritage shirts, a trend seen locally with sold-out heritage NRL jerseys and Australian-made vintage AFL wool guernseys. Socceroo Jackson Irvine wearing a retro Japan jersey in a picture he posted to social media. Jackson Irvine/Instagram International dealer Classic Football Shirts is perhaps the industry biggest player, growing from a Manchester student dorm online operation in 2006 into a global powerhouse with physical stores in the UK and US. In May 2024, American the private equity firm Chernin Group took a minority stake in the company with a £30.4 million growth equity investment. Analysts have valued the business at approaching £50 million ($94 million). Back home, Brisbane start-up Unwanted FC is turning heads around the globe with its very different approach. While they collect and sell vintage shirts, its founders, twins Kevin and Keith Chan, were inspired to upcycle unused or damaged kits after seeing the football industry’s wastage firsthand as interns at Adidas’s headquarters in Germany.

Advertisement

“Our jobs as interns were to destroy samples, we couldn’t even donate them,” says Kevin. They spoke about the conundrum with their aunt, a retired tailor, who helped them turn an old kit into a tote bag. Founders of Unwanted FC Kevin and Keith Chan at their new Sydney store. Steven Siewert After launching in 2018, their business has grown to upcycle kits into boot bags, toiletry kits, hats, women’s crop tops and shirts with shirring, and now, business shirts and ties. They recently opened a concept store in Sydney. Manipulating the stretchy fabric is tricky, requiring several experienced garment technicians to sew the designs together. The Matildas’ popularity has generated immense interest from women looking to signal their affection for the game with unique items. Players including Ellie Carpenter modelling their upcycled garments on Instagram has boosted this and about half of Unwanted FC’s customers are now women, the brothers say. “They think they can get more use out of a side bag or a tote bag than a jersey ... it’s a different way to wear, it’s [more] accessible.” But altering jerseys can come at an emotional cost. At one point, the brothers pleaded with a customer who had sent in a rare 90s Arsenal sweatshirt to reconsider their request for it to be chopped up. “We just couldn’t cut it up, so instead of taking her money, we bought it off her,” says Kevin. Their work has caught the eye of global football royalty. Kevin recalls the moment he saw Spanish footballer and fashion icon Hector Bellerin photographed holding one of Unwanted FC’s reworked items. “I couldn’t sleep that night, I literally thought I was dreaming,” he says.

Many Phillip Island residents who oppose McDonald’s plans want the Bass Coast Shire to follow the lead of its British counterpart and reject the application for a 24-hour outlet. Say No to McDonald’s member Trevor Ryan said community concerns about the proposed outlet for Cowes ranged from environmental damage and health impacts to traffic and road safety issues – particularly for young children at the primary school just metres away. Opponents of the proposed McDonald’s outlet for Phillip Island fear fast food will bring litter that will be damaging for wildlife. Joe Armao He said the global hamburger chain would devastate the tourism destination’s food scene by taking business away from local operators. “Phillip Island’s appeal is built around distinctive local food, drink and visitor experiences,” Ryan said.

Advertisement

Related Article Diet Town and country: The bunfight over McDonald’s in two very different locations Opponents fighting McDonald’s in Cowes fear it will generate a wave of packaging litter that will compromise Phillip Island’s unique coastal wildlife. “Rubbish does not just blow into the next suburb, it blows into our ocean,” Ryan said. McDonald’s has applied to the Bass Coast Shire to operate 24/7 with a maximum of 50 seats. If approved, the outlet would be less than 20 metres from the boundary of Cowes Primary School and is directly opposite retirement home units. It would be the first McDonald’s outlet on Phillip Island. The application has triggered about 1000 objections lodged with the Bass Coast Shire council. By comparison, it has received 26 letters in support.

Advertisement

One of those supporting letters said a McDonald’s outlet would provide jobs for young people as well as somewhere to get coffee after 2pm and food after 8pm when other businesses have closed. Another supporting letter said the proposed site was beside a service station, making it a suitable location while also providing a food choice for emergency services and shift workers. A 7-Eleven outlet has been approved for that service station site. Geoff Moed and Trevor Ryan on the site of the proposed McDonald’s outlet in Cowes. Justin McManus However, an online petition opposing the McDonald’s outlet in Cowes has more than 5700 signatures. Cowes health and wellness coach Victoria McGregor-Dawson said Phillip Island did not need McDonald’s. She said the location directly opposite retirement units was particularly problematic.

Advertisement

“You’ve got the elderly people living here, and they’re going to be infringed upon by lights, noise, smell on every level,” she said. Later this month, the Bass Coast Shire will hold a public meeting to hear from residents about their views on the proposed McDonald’s outlet. Victoria McGregor-Dawson says there are few redeeming qualities for McDonald’s in Cowes. Justin McManus But councils have traditionally had little power to reject fast food planning applications. And when they do, the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal can overturn those decisions. A McDonald’s outlet is under construction in Northcote despite vehement protests from residents. The Victorian parliament has passed legislation giving councils new powers enabling them to consider the health implications of planning applications. Presently, councils cannot assess planning applications on health grounds.

Advertisement

Related Article Diet McDonald’s wants to open on a primary school’s doorstep. The school is far from happy But the new powers do not come into effect until October next year, and opponents of the proposed new outlets say the fast food giant is trying to ram through planning applications while it can exploit the existing rules. Residents have also mobilised against plans for a McDonald’s outlet in the gold-rush town of Castlemaine, which remains free of global fast food franchises. Mac Off Protect Castlemaine coordinator Vicki Anderson said the looming new laws were not strong enough, and needed to focus on the pattern of fast food operators setting up near schools. “We don’t consider the legislation strong enough to deal with this specific issue,” she said.

Advertisement

Anderson said McDonald’s had bought the site it intended to develop in Castlemaine, at the town’s arrival point, but was yet to submit a planning application to the local council. She said the proposed location was inappropriate for a fast food restaurant. “It’s a major walking, cycling and traffic route.” Sustain: The Australian Food Network executive director Nick Rose said McDonald’s was attempting to secure new outlets in Victoria before councils had the chance to block them. He said fast food corporations were targeting growth areas, often crowding out healthier options. “We have a public health problem in this state,” Rose said.

Advertisement

He argued communities had a right to live free of fast food outlets if they wished. “They want healthier food environments for themselves and their kids,” he said. “For me, it’s a question of democracy.” But McDonald’s asserts its outlets deliver numerous community benefits. A company spokesperson said one of its new outlets could generate investment of $3 million to $5 million, creating hundreds of jobs in construction and ongoing employment after opening. “When considering new restaurant locations, we assess a range of factors including zoning, population growth, traffic flow and accessibility, to ensure we can meet the needs of local communities,” the spokesperson said. McDonald’s opponents Geoff Moed and Trevor Ware in front of the school where the proposed outlet will be built. Justin McManus

Advertisement

The company said it valued community feedback and worked with councils to ensure development applications complied with planning laws and regulations. But Phillip Island Business Network member Geoff Moed disputed suggestions McDonald’s would deliver an economic boost to the community. He said the company used technology, including customer touch screens, to minimise staff numbers. “It’s a multinational company that sends the bulk of their money overseas,” Moed said.

Fremantle’s football boss has backed the club using “Wharfie Time” in the future despite the capitulation that followed its activation with just four minutes and 18 seconds remaining in the grand final. At that point, the Dockers had established a game high 17-point lead and had one hand on their first premiership cup. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
